report.summary: Voice vocabulary fixed: each room now understands "set the <room> to 20", "set the <room> to 21.5" and "<room> 21 and a half" (targets carried per phrase), plus ordinary "warm up"/"cool down"/"cancel"; the phrase list and each recognised English phrase are now logged. Builds at 2.94 MB, 20 % free.
decisions: The model was English all along (mn7_en, WakeNet wn9_hiesp); the message you saw was MultiNet's 'nothing matched' outcome, which it reports when the words spoken are not in the vocabulary — not a wrong-language model. The real defect was the vocabulary: every room only understood 21 / 21.5 / 22, so 'set the bathroom to 20' had no matching phrase.

Rather than parse a number out of text at runtime, each phrase now carries its target in its id (20, 21.5, 21-and-a-half) — the recogniser matches what was actually said, and the published value is exactly that. The relative commands became ordinary English ('warm up' / 'cool down' instead of 'plus one' / 'minus one').

Added observability so the next run answers 'did it hear me?': the phrase list is printed as the window opens and a match prints the recognised English text with its confidence. The front button's 'single click (no handler)' line is gone as well — that was the generated weak hook's log, now routed to the product's push-to-talk.

openQuestions: MultiNet's mn7_en takes the words it is given in a fixed grammar; if a room is renamed on the settings page, the vocabulary is fixed until reboot — which happens on the next power cycle at the latest.
Numbers other than 20 / 21.5 / 21-and-a-half are only reachable with the on-screen −/+; more spoken numbers would mean more phrases (MultiNet's list is finite and every phrase costs model memory).
